messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Vignette:
At 67, Matiu arrived for treatment looking like a man who had spent a long time trying to keep himself composed. He was widowed, lived alone, and worked as an interior designer, a role that once suited his eye for order and detail but had become harder to sustain. Originally from an Oceania background and now settled in the United States, he described himself as someone who had always preferred calm, elegant spaces, the kind where he could choose materials, move furniture, and think clearly. That preference for control had shifted sharply after the period when he was held captive abroad, an experience he still struggled to tell in sequence.

Matiu spoke of the captivity as a time in which ordinary movement, privacy, and speech were taken from him. When he tried to describe it, he repeatedly lost the thread, circling back to fragments and then stopping, saying he could not get it out “properly.” He could recall what had happened in a factual sense, but at times the memory felt strangely numb to him, as if it had happened to someone else. At other times the recollection arrived with a different force altogether: without warning, a picture of the event would intrude into his mind in the middle of an ordinary day, and he would be left shaken by how suddenly it appeared. He also noticed that some parts of the memory returned with sound attached. In particular, shouting in Arabic would sometimes surface in his head exactly as he had heard it during the frightening period, not as a vague impression but as an auditory echo that made him feel as if he were back in the same atmosphere of threat.

The specific quality of those sounds mattered. In the place where he had been confined, raised voices in Arabic had been one of the signals that something was about to happen, and his body now seemed to recognize them before he could think. If he passed people speaking loudly in Arabic at a restaurant, on the street, or near a job site, he would tense immediately and feel a rush of fear and other strong negative emotions he had trouble settling. He found that he began scanning rooms for exits and measuring distance automatically. He was most comfortable when his back was against a wall and he could see the whole room, because anything else left him feeling exposed. He described this not as a choice but as a condition he needed in order to breathe normally.

His day-to-day life had become organized around not being trapped. Enclosed or confined spaces were particularly hard for him. Elevators, small meeting rooms, and narrow interior spaces could make him feel cornered, and over time he began avoiding them whenever possible. He also started avoiding going to work or study in the way he used to, even though his profession depended on being present in buildings, offices, and client spaces. As an interior designer, he once spent his days moving from one site to another, but now he would sometimes decline appointments or delay visits if he thought he might be stuck in a small room or unable to orient himself easily. This had altered both his work rhythm and his confidence with clients, and he knew it.

Matiu also described an unusual habit that had developed before any interaction, whether with a client, a contractor, or even a shop assistant. He rehearsed what he would say in advance, sometimes several times, as though preparing for a test. He explained that when he felt emotionally vulnerable, he became aware of that vulnerability as danger in itself. Part of him expected that if he were not carefully composed, he might be overwhelmed, misunderstood, or lose control of the exchange. The rehearsing offered him a sense of protection, though it also made him feel less spontaneous and more distant from others.

When he spoke of the years after the captivity, his face would sometimes go blank in a way that matched his description of numb recollection. He was capable of working, of keeping appointments, and of presenting himself neatly, but these efforts seemed to sit alongside a persistent sense that his body had not fully accepted that the danger was over. He said that before he had time to think, his body would react to danger on its own, which was especially disconcerting because it made him feel undone by something he could not reason away. Since his wife’s death, he had had even fewer natural buffers in daily life, and he now found that the isolation of living alone could leave him more aware of how often he was arranging his world around threat.

He came for help only after noticing how much smaller his life had become: fewer site visits, fewer spontaneous conversations, and more time spent planning how to sit, where to stand, and what to say. He was not seeking to be made fearless. What brought him in was the fear that his world was becoming organized entirely around staying protected, and his hope was that he might learn to explain what happened without losing the thread, to sit in a room without needing the wall behind him, and to move through his work without feeling that every loud voice or enclosed space was pulling him back toward captivity.
